Should JustEat keep funding free professional photography?¶

Part 1: experiment design

Introduction¶

The professional photography service started as a growth lever and became a multimillion-euro operation running across hundreds of cities. Management wants to know whether it still pays for itself, and the Data Science team has been asked to design the analysis that answers it.

The context has moved since the service launched. Customers order online without needing to be persuaded, restaurants have good smartphone cameras, and the counterfactual to a professional shoot is no longer "no photos" but "a phone and a tutorial". So the honest version of the question is not "do good photos sell food", which they plainly do, but "does our paying for them still generate more margin than it consumes".

This notebook works that question into a design. It starts by writing down what the decision actually requires, which turns out to be more specific than the brief implies, then asks how much of that the existing data can supply, and builds the experiments from whatever is left over. The simulations here exist to show what each design choice buys us and what the output will look like when real data arrives. They are not findings. Every number is either simulated or an illustrative placeholder, and is flagged as such.

1. What the decision actually requires¶

Before designing anything I want to write down the arithmetic that a "yes" would have to satisfy, because the shape of that expression determines what has to be measured and therefore what has to be randomised.

The service is worth funding for a given restaurant if the margin its photos generate over their useful life exceeds what the shoot cost:

$$\eta \times \tau_{\text{LATE}} \times \text{GMV} \times r \times m \times L \;>\; C_{\text{var}}$$

Nine terms, and they are not equally well understood. Setting them out side by side is worth the effort, because it makes visible how lopsided our knowledge of them is.

Symbol Term What it means Owner Where it comes from Status today
$\eta$ incrementality Share of a restaurant's gain that is genuinely new demand rather than orders taken from a neighbouring restaurant on the same platform Data Science Randomised variation in how many restaurants in a competitive set are treated Never measured. On a marketplace a restaurant's gain can be another restaurant's loss, so this is the largest unknown in the expression and the one that decides the answer
$\tau_{\text{LATE}}$ effect on adopters Percentage uplift in an adopting restaurant's own GMV caused by having professional photos Data Science Randomised offer, with adoption instrumented by the offer Observational estimates exist, but restaurants request the service rather than being assigned it, so they are almost certainly inflated
$\text{take-up}$ adoption rate Share of restaurants that accept when offered. Converts a per-adopter effect into a per-offer cost, and drives sample size Ops and Sales Directly observed once offers are randomised Historical rates exist but have never been pulled by segment
$\text{GMV}$ monthly platform GMV The base the uplift applies to. Must be segment-level, since a percentage uplift on a €3k restaurant is not the same decision as on a €20k one Finance Existing platform data Known in aggregate, needs segmenting
$r$ take rate Commission share of GMV Finance Contractual Known
$m$ contribution margin Margin on commission revenue after payment processing, support and refunds Finance Management accounts Known, needs confirming for this use
$L$ effective asset life Discounted months over which the uplift persists, before menu churn, restaurant churn and novelty decay erode it Data Science Long-run follow-up, bounded above by menu turnover The most fragile assumption. Everything downstream is linear in it
$C_{\text{var},s}$ cost per shoot Fully loaded: photographer fee, travel, editing, storage, scheduling, and the account-management time to arrange it Finance and Ops Activity-based costing Partially known, usually understated, and unlikely to be constant across markets
$C_{\text{fix}}$ programme overhead Annual cost of having the programme at all: the operations team, the photographer network, the booking platform Finance Management accounts Missing from the expression above

Two things about that inequality need saying before it is used, because it is written from the point of view of a restaurant that already has the photos.

It is a per-shoot condition, so $\tau$ is the effect on adopters. That is the quantity usually called a local average treatment effect, local because it is identified only on the restaurants whose adoption decision the offer actually changes. It is the right term here because $C_{\text{var}}$ is incurred per shoot, so both sides of the inequality are already conditioned on a shoot having happened.

But management cannot buy adoptions, only offers. The lever is the offer, and the quantity attached to it is the intention-to-treat effect, the per-offer version of the same thing: $\text{ITT}_s = \text{take-up}_s \times \tau_s$. That relation is why take-up earns a row in the table despite being absent from the inequality above. It is the exchange rate between the number the experiment identifies most cleanly and the number the decision is actually made in, and forgetting it is how a programme gets approved on an adopter-level uplift it will never achieve across a population.

Writing the portfolio condition over offers rather than shoots makes both visible at once. Here $s$ indexes a partition of the eligible base into segments, mutually exclusive and jointly exhaustive so that every restaurant is counted once and only once, and $N_s$ is the number of restaurants in segment $s$ we would offer the service to. What those segments should actually be is a design decision in its own right, and one I come back to once there is an experiment capable of resolving them:

$$\sum_{s \,\in\, \text{segments}} N_s \, \text{take-up}_s \left( \eta_s \, \tau_s \, \text{GMV}_s \, r \, m \, L_s - C_{\text{var},s} \right) \;>\; C_{\text{fix}}$$

The last row of the table is what forces the condition to be written this way at all. A per-shoot inequality quietly assumes the programme has no fixed cost, which contradicts the brief's own description of a multimillion-euro operation that is a challenge to manage. With $C_{\text{fix}}$ on the right, the decision stops being a per-restaurant test and becomes a portfolio question.

Three things follow immediately, and they shape everything after this section.

The subscripts are not decoration. Both $\eta$ and $\tau$ should be expected to vary by segment, and in opposite directions in at least one case: a thin market has few substitutes, so a gain there is more likely to be genuinely new demand (high $\eta$), while a dense urban market is mostly share-shifting (low $\eta$). If that holds, the segments with the smallest measured uplift may be the ones with the highest incrementality. An average would hide it.

Which terms lack a subscript is just as much a claim. I have left $r$ and $m$ without one, which is defensible if commission and margin are contractually uniform and worth checking if they are not. $C_{\text{var},s}$ is the one that deserves the most scrutiny here. The cost row includes photographer travel, and travel is precisely what differs between a dense city and a thin market, so a single number cannot be right. That matters more than it looks, because it pushes against $\eta$: the thin markets where a gain is most likely to be genuinely incremental are also the ones where reaching the restaurant costs most. The two effects work in opposite directions and only a segmented cost figure can tell us which wins.

All three terms owned by Data Science are unreliable, in two different ways. $\eta$ and $L$ have never been measured at all, and $\tau$ has been measured badly, through the observational estimates the next section takes apart. That is the whole job of the experiments. Everything else on the list belongs to Finance or to Ops, and is mostly a matter of asking the right person rather than running anything, which is why the closing section is a list of asks rather than a second design.

A "kill" answer and a "shrink" answer look completely different in this expression. Killing sets the left side to zero and recovers $C_{\text{fix}}$. Shrinking to the profitable segments keeps $C_{\text{fix}}$ while cutting $N_s$, which only helps if the surviving segments generate enough to carry the overhead alone. I come back to this at the end, and it changes the recommendation.

2. Can the data we already have answer any of this?¶

The brief reports two findings from the programme's early days: customers were more likely to order food with professional photographs, and restaurants were able to charge more for it. Both are presented as evidence that the service works. Neither can carry that weight, and it is worth being precise about why before spending money on experiments.

Restaurants request the photographer. That single fact creates three problems at once. Self-selection, because operator quality drives both the decision to ask and the tendency to grow anyway. Reverse causality, because a restaurant is most likely to ask when demand is already climbing. And survivorship, because restaurants that churned never got photos and never appear in a "twelve months after the shoot" cut of the data.

All three push in the same direction. The simulation below builds a world where the true effect on adopters is exactly +8%, then asks what each analysis method would report.

In [2]:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch, FancyArrowPatch

# ---------------- simulation ----------------
def one_rep(seed, n=3000, T=12, t0=6, tau=0.08):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    mom = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
    base, growth = 8.0 + 0.45*mom, 0.004 + 0.010*mom
    t = np.arange(T)
    noise, unit = rng.normal(0, .25, (n, T)), rng.normal(0, .6, (n, 1))
    post = t >= t0
    D = rng.random(n) < 1/(1+np.exp(-(-0.6 + 1.3*mom)))
    Y = base[:, None] + growth[:, None]*t + unit + noise + tau*(D[:, None] & post)
    pre_m, post_m = Y[:, :t0].mean(1), Y[:, t0:].mean(1)
    naive = post_m[D].mean() - post_m[~D].mean()
    ba = post_m[D].mean() - pre_m[D].mean()
    did = naive - (pre_m[D].mean() - pre_m[~D].mean())
    dec = pd.qcut(pre_m, 10, labels=False, duplicates="drop")
    ms = [ (post_m[(dec==d)&D].mean()-post_m[(dec==d)&~D].mean())
          -(pre_m[(dec==d)&D].mean()-pre_m[(dec==d)&~D].mean())
          for d in np.unique(dec) if D[dec==d].sum()>5 and (~D[dec==d]).sum()>5]
    Z = rng.random(n) < .5
    A = Z & (rng.random(n) < 1/(1+np.exp(-(-0.2 + 1.1*mom))))
    Y2 = base[:, None] + growth[:, None]*t + unit + noise + tau*(A[:, None] & post)
    p2, q2 = Y2[:, t0:].mean(1), Y2[:, :t0].mean(1)
    itt = (p2[Z].mean()-p2[~Z].mean()) - (q2[Z].mean()-q2[~Z].mean())
    return dict(naive=naive, ba=ba, did=did, matched=np.mean(ms),
                itt=itt, late=itt/(A[Z].mean()-A[~Z].mean()))

reps = pd.DataFrame([one_rep(s) for s in range(300)])

# ---------------- figure ----------------

The naive comparison overstates by a factor of seven and a half, and the three observational corrections below it each strip out one layer without reaching the truth.

Before and after uses each adopter as its own control, which eliminates every fixed difference between restaurants at a stroke. What it cannot touch is time. The adopters were on a rising path anyway, and six months of that growth ends up folded into the estimate.

Difference-in-differences attacks the same problem from the other side, netting out whatever the control group did over the same window. That removes the level gap, which is why the estimate falls from +60.6% to +13.9%, but it only removes the part of the trend the two groups have in common. The differential part, the fact that adopters were growing faster than controls to begin with, survives untouched. This is the method most likely to be sitting in the current business case.

Matched DiD is the obvious repair: compare adopters only against non-adopters of similar size, by stratifying on pre-period GMV before differencing. It barely helps, moving the estimate to +13.0%, and the reason is worth spelling out because it is the whole argument for randomising. Within any given size stratum, the restaurants that go on to request photos still have systematically better prospects than those that do not. Two restaurants of equal size today can be one solid business at its ceiling and one smaller one on the way up, and it is the second that picks up the phone. Matching equalises what you match on and leaves everything you cannot observe exactly where it was.

The natural objection is that we should stratify on the pre-period trend rather than the level, which is essentially what a parallel-trends check amounts to. That does no better here, and for an instructive reason: six months of noisy monthly data cannot identify a restaurant's underlying growth rate, so the strata end up close to random with respect to the thing that actually drives the bias. A parallel-trends diagnostic is usually underpowered, and passing one is weaker evidence than it looks.

Only randomisation equalises what we cannot see, which is why the two randomised estimates are the only ones in the chart that land where they should.

Two things in that chart are worth dwelling on.

The gap between the two randomised estimates is not noise. The ITT of +3.7% is the effect of offering the service and the LATE of +8.1% is the effect on restaurants that accept, and the ratio between them is the take-up rate. Both are useful and they answer different questions. Management controls the offer, not the adoption, so the ITT is the policy-relevant number even though the LATE is the one everyone will want to quote.

And the brief's second finding deserves a second look rather than a nod. "Restaurants were able to charge more" is not unambiguously good news for JustEat. Higher menu prices raise commission per order but depress conversion and, over a longer horizon, customer retention. A GMV win driven by price is a different business outcome from one driven by volume, and only one of them compounds. Any readout has to decompose GMV into orders, basket size and a price index rather than reporting the product and calling it growth.

3. The term nobody measures¶

Section 1 put $\eta$ at the front of the expression and marked it as never measured. This is where I want to spend the design budget, because it is the difference between a right answer and a confidently wrong one.

Standard A/B testing assumes that one unit's treatment does not affect another unit's outcome. In a two-sided marketplace with a roughly fixed pool of hungry customers in a given area on a given evening, that assumption is simply false. When a treated restaurant's listing becomes more attractive, some of the orders it wins are new (a customer who would have cooked at home) and some are taken from the restaurant two streets away, which is also on JustEat and also paying commission. The platform earns the first kind and nothing at all from the second.

So $\eta$ is the fraction of an attractiveness gain that is genuinely incremental. A restaurant-level A/B test measures the full attractiveness effect $\beta$. The platform earns $\eta\beta$. The simulation below shows both, and shows how varying how many restaurants in a competitive set are treated separates them.

In [3]:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)

BETA = 0.12          # true effect of photos on a listing's attractiveness
ETA  = 0.30          # share of an attractiveness gain that is genuinely new demand
K    = 25            # restaurants per delivery zone
BREAKEVEN = 4.6      # % uplift needed to cover the cost of a shoot (derived later)


def zone_block(n_zones, p, beta=BETA, eta=ETA, k=K, seed=0):
    """Simulate n_zones delivery zones in which a fraction p of restaurants are treated."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    a = r.normal(0, 0.5, (n_zones, k))                 # intrinsic appeal
    T = r.random((n_zones, k)) < p
    v = a + beta * T
    s = np.exp(v) / np.exp(v).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    D = 1000 * np.exp(eta * beta * T.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True))   # market expansion
    orders = s * D * np.exp(r.normal(0, 0.05, (n_zones, k)))
    return orders, T


sats = np.array([0, .125, .25, .375, .5, .625, .75, .875, 1.0])
N_ZONES = 4000
rows = []
for i, p in enumerate(sats):
    o, T = zone_block(N_ZONES, p, seed=100 + i)
    rows.append(dict(
        sat=p,
        treated=np.log(o[T]).mean() if T.any() else np.nan,
        control=np.log(o[~T]).mean() if (~T).any() else np.nan,
        market=np.log(o.sum(axis=1)).mean(),
    ))
res = {k: np.array([r[k] for r in rows]) for k in rows[0]}
base_unit, base_mkt = res["control"][0], res["market"][0]
treated = (np.exp(res["treated"] - base_unit) - 1) * 100
control = (np.exp(res["control"] - base_unit) - 1) * 100
market  = (np.exp(res["market"] - base_mkt) - 1) * 100

fig, (ax, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13.4, 5.4),
                              gridspec_kw=dict(wspace=0.24, width_ratios=[1.05, 1]))

# ---------------- Panel A: saturation curves ----------------
ax.plot(sats * 100, treated, "o-", color=ORANGE, lw=2.4, ms=6.5, label="restaurants that got photos")
ax.plot(sats * 100, control, "o-", color=RED, lw=2.4, ms=6.5, label="their untreated neighbours")
ax.plot(sats * 100, market, "o-", color=INK, lw=3.0, ms=7, label="the zone as a whole  ← what JustEat earns")
ax.axhline(0, color=MUTED, lw=1.0)

            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=BLUE, lw=2.0))
ax.annotate(f"what a restaurant-level A/B test measures\n≈ {treated[4]-control[4]:.1f}%   (direct effect + stolen share)",
            xy=(50, 8.2), xytext=(56, 14.6), fontsize=9.3, color=BLUE, weight="bold",
            linespacing=1.35, ha="center",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=BLUE, lw=1.4,
                            connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.2"))

A/B estimate  : 11.86 %
platform gain : 3.68 %
overstatement : 3.23 x
break-even eta: 37.5 %

Panel A is the design in one picture. The gap between the orange and red lines is what a conventional A/B test reports. The slope of the black line is what JustEat actually earns. Both come out of the same experiment, and estimating $\eta$ is then a regression of cluster-total log orders on treatment saturation, with the slope divided by $\beta$.

Panel B is the uncomfortable part. On the illustrative economics of section 8, the service pays for itself only if $\eta$ exceeds roughly 37%, and we currently have no idea whether it does. That single parameter is worth more than any refinement of the effect size.

A note on how the competitive set is defined, because the intuitive choice is the wrong one. The obvious construction is geographic: delivery radius crossed with cuisine. It fails in a way that matters. Delivery radii overlap, so restaurants do not partition into zones; they form a network. Two restaurants compete to the extent that they appear in the same customer's choice set, which is something we log directly. The right construction is to build a co-consideration graph from search and browse data (an edge weighted by how often two restaurants are viewed in the same session) and cluster that, using community detection, so that within-cluster substitution is high and between-cluster substitution is as low as we can make it. Geography is a proxy for this graph and a mediocre one, particularly in dense cities where a customer's realistic choice set spans several neighbourhoods.

This is not a cosmetic change. If clusters leak, treated and control clusters cannibalise each other, the measured spillover is attenuated and $\eta$ comes out too high, which biases the whole analysis back toward the flattering answer. The leakage rate is measurable from the same graph, so it should be reported alongside the estimate rather than assumed away.

4. The design that follows¶

With $\eta$ and $\tau$ established as the terms that need randomisation, the rest of the design falls out of a short list of things that cannot be learned from the same experiment.

No single experiment answers the question. The fast ones lack external validity, the valid ones lack power, and only one of them measures the substitution that decides whether any of it is profitable. So there are five tracks, sequenced so the cheap reads de-risk the expensive ones.

Track A, restaurant-level randomised encouragement¶

The workhorse. Randomise restaurants, grouped by owner rather than by listing, because owners with several sites apply what they learn across all of them and owners talk to each other. Stratify with covariate-constrained randomisation on city, cuisine, pre-period GMV decile and tenure. Estimate ITT with log(GMV) ~ Z + strata + CUPED(pre-period GMV) and errors clustered on owner; estimate the LATE with two-stage least squares using the offer as the instrument.

Three arms rather than two. The obvious design is offer against no offer. But the offer is delivered by an account manager, and an account-manager conversation is itself an intervention: attention, a reminder that the platform exists, possibly a nudge on pricing or opening hours. A two-arm design bundles photography with salesmanship and reports the total as a photography effect. Adding a self-serve arm, where the service is surfaced in the account with no human contact, separates the two. It also happens to test the cheapest possible delivery mechanism, which matters if the answer turns out to be "keep it but stop staffing it".

The exclusion restriction that the IV rests on is then testable rather than assumed. Compare restaurants that were offered and declined against control: if the offer alone moves GMV, the LATE is contaminated and we report ITT only.

One thing to be careful about. The eligible population is restaurants that do not currently have professional photos, which is a selected group: they either declined before or were never asked. The LATE therefore generalises to compliers within that population, not to the installed base. The installed base is a separate question and only Track C touches it.

Track B, saturation randomisation¶

Co-consideration clusters are assigned to have 0, 25, 50, 75 or 100% of their members offered the service, and within a cluster, which members get the offer is randomised. One experiment, two contrasts: the within-cluster contrast gives the restaurant-level effect and the across-cluster contrast gives the spillover.

$\eta$ should be estimated per segment rather than pooled, for the reason given in section 1. That is expensive in clusters, so in practice I would power for a thin-market against dense-market split and treat any finer breakdown as exploratory.

Track C, geo switch-off¶

Matched pairs of cities, with the service withdrawn for new requests in one of each pair. This is the only track that measures the decision actually on the table, including the effects nothing else can see: restaurant churn, sales-team behaviour, and the operations cost that would actually be released. It is slow and low-powered, so it confirms sign and order of magnitude rather than fine detail. It is also the only track that says anything about the installed base.

Track D, customer-side listing experiment¶

Within restaurants that hold both professional and standard image sets, randomise which customers see which. Enormous power, reads in four weeks, and it is the only place we can cleanly measure the expectation-mismatch risk: professional photography may set a bar the kitchen cannot clear. If "item not as described" refunds rise, part of the GMV gain is illusory and part of the retention effect is negative. It also splits new against returning customers, which speaks directly to $\eta$: if the gain is acquisition rather than redistribution, the cannibalisation correction is too harsh.

Track E, cost-effectiveness arms¶

Control, a self-serve toolkit with guidelines, AI enhancement of existing photos, a 50% co-pay, and the full free service. This reframes the brief. Even if the full service is unprofitable, a toolkit at five per cent of the cost capturing sixty per cent of the value would be an excellent outcome, and the co-pay arm reveals whether restaurants place any value on the service at all, which no amount of GMV analysis can tell us.

One cross-cutting decision: the ranking loop¶

If search ranking consumes conversion rate as a feature, a treated listing gets an algorithmic boost on top of the imagery effect, and that boost is zero-sum at platform level. Rather than choosing between freezing ranking and letting it adapt, the design can have both and use the difference. Track D runs with ranking features frozen, which isolates the imagery effect on conversion. Tracks A, B and C run with ranking live, which measures the total effect a real rollout would produce. The gap between them is the algorithmic amplification, and it belongs on the cannibalised side of the ledger rather than the incremental side.

5. Can we power it?¶

Three constraints, in increasing order of how much trouble they cause.

In [5]:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

ALPHA, POWER = 0.05, 0.80
Kz = stats.norm.ppf(1 - ALPHA / 2) + stats.norm.ppf(POWER)

def mde(sigma, n_per_arm, r2=0.0):
    """Two-sample MDE on a log outcome, after variance reduction of R^2."""
    return Kz * sigma * np.sqrt(1 - r2) * np.sqrt(2 / n_per_arm)

Track A is comfortably feasible. With CUPED on pre-period GMV plus stratification, which should give an R-squared around 0.8 for a quantity as autocorrelated as restaurant GMV, roughly 3,850 restaurants per arm detects a 2% ITT. That is a small fraction of the eligible base, and the three-arm version costs about 50% more units than the two-arm one, which is affordable.

Take-up is the binding constraint, and the fix is operational rather than statistical. Sample size scales with the square of the inverse take-up rate: at 15% take-up we need 10,700 restaurants per arm, at 60% we need 670. Raising take-up from 15% to 30% is worth more than quadrupling the sample and costs less. This is worth saying to the ops team before it is worth saying to the statistics.

Geo tests only work with heavy variance reduction. Raw city-level GMV gives a useless 14% MDE at 100 cities per arm. Pre-period CUPED brings it to 3.1% and synthetic control methods to 1.4%. Since the effect we are hunting is around 2.4%, Track C is viable only with that machinery, which makes it a build requirement rather than an analysis afterthought.

On duration. Whole weeks, always. Beyond that, three clocks run at different speeds: the take-up lag, since request to shoot to live listing is weeks rather than days; effect accumulation through ranking, repeat customers and reviews; and novelty decay. The 26-week primary read is set by the second.

The third clock is a problem I do not have a clean answer to. The economics in section 8 assume an asset life of 24 months, but the longest follow-up in this design runs to 78 weeks, which is 18. So the design cannot verify its own most fragile assumption. Two partial mitigations: bound $L$ above using menu turnover, which is answerable from the database this week and tells us how long a photo of a given dish stays relevant at all, and publish the primary read with an explicit sensitivity band on $L$ rather than a point estimate.

6. What we measure on both sides¶

Impact "on restaurants and customers" means a full metric tree on both sides, not a GMV number and some improvisation.

Restaurant side. Monthly GMV is primary, decomposed into orders, basket size and a menu price index for the reason given in section 2. Items listed with photos is the dose measure, which tells us whether the shoot actually changed the listing. Ninety-day restaurant churn is a guardrail and possibly more than that: if the service is mainly buying supply retention rather than order uplift, the entire calculation should be rebuilt around restaurant lifetime value. Engagement measures (hours online, menu edits, logins) tell us whether the service deepens the relationship, and restaurant CSAT is the guardrail on withdrawing a free perk.

Customer side. Session-to-order conversion on exposed listings is primary for Track D. The split between new and returning customers is the mechanism measure that feeds $\eta$. Basket size, items per order and 28-day repeat rate are secondary. Listings viewed before ordering is a genuine customer benefit worth tracking. And "not as described" refunds and complaints is a guardrail I have not seen measured in any photography business case, despite being the obvious failure mode of making food look better than it arrives.

Platform. Net cluster-level GMV, which is the only truly incremental number, commission revenue, and contribution margin net of both the variable and the fixed photography cost.

Guardrails are tested one-sided against a pre-agreed non-inferiority margin and are not swept into the multiple-comparison correction. A correction that makes it harder to detect harm is a correction pointed the wrong way.

7. Threats to validity, and what each one needs¶

Before launch. An A/A test for two weeks, which validates the assignment and logging pipeline, measures the real variance and intra-cluster correlation for the power calculations, and checks that the false positive rate is actually 5%. Pre-registration of the primary metric, MDE, stopping rule, subgroups and decision rule, circulated before a single unit is assigned, because without it the segmentation in section 9 is indistinguishable from p-hacking. And covariate-constrained randomisation rather than post-hoc adjustment.

During. A daily sample-ratio-mismatch check, where any deviation halts the readout and triggers a pipeline investigation rather than an interpretation. Sequential testing with group-sequential boundaries or always-valid confidence sequences, because leadership will look weekly and the only choice is whether the statistics survive it. And blinding where possible: if account managers are the delivery channel, randomise at AM-portfolio level, or the AM's enthusiasm becomes a confounder and we measure salesmanship rather than photography. The three-arm design in section 4 is partly a response to this same threat.

In analysis. Analyse at the unit of randomisation, with errors clustered on owner for Track A, cluster for Track B and city for Track C. ITT primary and always reported with the take-up rate beside it. Benjamini-Hochberg across secondary metrics. And include restaurants that churned, entering the analysis with GMV of zero, because dropping them re-introduces exactly the survivorship bias the experiment was built to avoid.

On ethics, which is not a footnote here. Withholding a free service from control restaurants is a real cost to real businesses, and Track C goes further by withdrawing an existing service in whole cities. Four mitigations: keep the control window short and the control arm as small as power allows; use a waitlist so control receives the service after the measurement window; never withdraw photos already delivered; and cap Track C to cities representing a small share of platform GMV, with the downside sized and pre-agreed rather than discovered. Track C is the version leadership is most likely to accept, because withdrawing a service for new requests is a genuine business trial of the policy under consideration rather than the removal of an established benefit, but it must be reversible and it must be communicated.

8. Putting the numbers back into the formula¶

An experiment that ends in a p-value has not finished. The decision rule needs the unit economics from section 1, and it needs them agreed with Finance before the readout, so that the threshold is not renegotiated once the answer is known.

The assumptions below are illustrative placeholders for the real figures.

In [6]:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ---------- unit economics (illustrative, to be replaced with finance's numbers) ----------
GMV_M   = 8_000.0    # €/month GMV of a typical restaurant
TAKE    = 0.14       # commission rate
CM      = 0.60       # contribution margin on commission revenue
COST    = 450.0      # fully-loaded cost of one shoot
LIFE    = 24         # months the asset is live
DECAY   = 0.04       # monthly decay of the uplift
DISC    = 0.008      # monthly discount rate

months = np.arange(LIFE)
EFF_MONTHS = np.sum(np.exp(-DECAY * months) / (1 + DISC) ** months)
VALUE_PER_PP = GMV_M * 0.01 * TAKE * CM * EFF_MONTHS      # € per +1pp of uplift
BREAKEVEN = COST / VALUE_PER_PP                            # in percentage points

Panel A is the argument of this whole notebook in one chart. Each design choice strips out a layer of illusion, and the answer crosses the break-even line on the way down. Whether the service is profitable depends entirely on whether we correct for cannibalisation, which is why $\eta$ was worth building a whole track around.

Panel B puts uncertainty on it. On these assumptions a shoot pays for itself 20% of the time with a median loss of about €200, but the 90% interval runs from -€399 to +€322. That is not a business with a clear answer. It is a business with enormous heterogeneity, which is the actual finding and points somewhere more useful than yes or no.

One methodological note on how this should be reported. The decision is not "is the effect significantly different from zero", it is "is the expected contribution above the hurdle rate". Those are different questions and the second is better served by a Bayesian posterior than a p-value. Pre-register the hurdle and report $P(\text{net contribution} > \text{hurdle})$ by segment, so that the readout hands leadership a probability of being right rather than an invitation to argue about significance.

9. Heterogeneity, and the question the per-shoot formula hides¶

Segments chosen from the mechanism rather than from the data: existing image quality, since the counterfactual matters most there and a restaurant with decent phone photos has little to gain in 2023; market thickness, which drives $\eta$ directly; cuisine visual salience, sushi and desserts against groceries and convenience; tenure, since new listings have no review base and lean harder on imagery; and average order value, since the same percentage uplift is worth more.

peak coverage 44 % -> EUR 20.5 m
full coverage 100% -> EUR -1.7 m

Panel A is why the average is the wrong summary. Returns per shoot run from +€980 to -€920, and a programme evaluated on its mean is being judged on a number that describes almost none of its population.

Panel B is where section 1 comes back. The black curve is the cumulative contribution as coverage extends from the best-returning segment down to the worst, and it peaks at +€20.5m at 44% coverage before falling to -€1.7m if the service is given to everyone. That is the targeting argument, and on its own it says: do not kill this, shrink it.

Then the overhead lines say something the per-shoot formula could not. The coverage that maximises return does not depend on $C_{\text{fix}}$, but whether the programme is worth running at all entirely does. At €6m of annual overhead the targeted programme nets €14.5m and is clearly worth keeping. At €20m it nets €0.5m, which is indistinguishable from zero once you account for the uncertainty in every term feeding it, and the honest recommendation flips to closure. Nobody has told us which of those worlds we are in, and the figure is not in the material provided.

This is the single most important thing I would change about how the question was framed. It was posed as a question about effect size, and effect size turns out not to determine the answer on its own.

A warning attached to the targeting conclusion. Segment-level effects are where experiments go to die. The discipline required is: pre-register a small set of segments and report those as confirmatory; explore further with causal forests or an X-learner on honestly split samples; and treat any discovered targeting policy as a hypothesis, validated in a second randomised wave that randomises the policy itself rather than the treatment, before it is rolled out. Skipping that last step is how organisations end up deploying an expensive targeting rule fitted to noise.

There is also a power consequence I should be explicit about. This design is powered to detect an average effect, not to resolve eight segments. Wave one gives the average and a coarse split, wave two validates the policy. Presenting wave one as a segment-level answer would be overreaching.

10. Conclusions¶

The existing evidence cannot support the existing business case. Restaurants select into the service, and they do it when demand is already rising. In simulation that turns a true +8% into a reported +60%, and difference-in-differences only claws it back to +14%. Whatever the programme is worth, it is not what the current numbers say.

One unmeasured parameter decides the answer. Because JustEat is a marketplace, a restaurant-level effect and a platform-level effect are different quantities, and in simulation they differ by a factor of three. The service pays for itself only if incrementality exceeds roughly 37%, and nobody has measured it. Measuring $\eta$ is worth more than any refinement of the effect size, and it needs a saturation design over co-consideration clusters, not a conventional A/B test.

The design is five tracks because no single experiment is both valid and affordable. Restaurant encouragement gives the effect on adopters and, in its three-arm form, separates photography from salesmanship. Saturation gives incrementality. The geo switch-off gives the total policy effect including supply retention. The customer-side test gives the mechanism and the expectation-mismatch risk in four weeks. The cost-effectiveness arms ask whether a toolkit at a fraction of the cost captures most of the value.

"Keep or kill" is the wrong question, but "shrink" is not automatically the right answer. Returns per shoot span €1,900 across segments. Serving everyone loses €1.7m a year while serving the best-returning 44% generates €20.5m before overhead. Whether that survives overhead depends on a number nobody has given us, and at €20m of annual programme cost the targeted programme is indistinguishable from closure.

What I would tell management today, before any of this runs. The answer to "is it worth it" is currently unknowable, not negative, and the reason is that three of the terms in the decision are unmeasured and one is missing from the framing entirely. The cheapest useful thing we could do this quarter is not an experiment at all: it is to establish the fixed overhead, pull take-up rates by segment, and measure menu turnover to bound the asset life. Those three numbers cost days rather than quarters, and they may narrow the decision enough to change what we bother randomising.

11. What I need before this can start¶

From Finance, and this is the blocking item. The annual fixed cost of running the programme, separated from the per-shoot cost. Section 9 shows the recommendation flipping between "shrink and keep" and "close" across a plausible range of that number, so no amount of experimental rigour substitutes for it. Alongside it, the fully loaded per-shoot cost including operations and account-management time, and confirmation of the contribution margin on commission for this use.

From Ops and Sales. Historical take-up rates by segment, which set the sample size, and an honest view of whether take-up can be moved, since section 5 shows that is worth more than sample size.

From Engineering. Confirmation of whether search ranking consumes conversion rate as a feature, which determines whether the ranking decomposition in section 4 is necessary or moot. And access to session-level co-view data, without which Track B falls back to the geographic proxy I argued against in section 3.

From the database, answerable this week. Menu turnover, which bounds the asset life from above and is the cheapest way to constrain the most fragile assumption in the model.

Limitations, and what would change my mind¶

  • If $\eta$ is high, particularly in thin markets, the blanket programme may be profitable after all and my central framing overcorrects. Track B settles it.
  • If the gain is customer acquisition rather than share-shifting, the cannibalisation correction is too harsh. Track D's new-against-returning split is the test and it reads in four weeks.
  • If restaurant churn rises materially when the service is withdrawn, the value of the programme is supply retention rather than order uplift, and the whole calculation should be rebuilt around restaurant lifetime value rather than GMV.
  • Asset life is the weakest assumption and the design cannot fully verify it, since the follow-up runs to 18 months against an assumed 24. The primary read should carry an explicit sensitivity band rather than a point estimate.
  • Cluster definition is the main threat to Track B. If co-consideration clusters leak, spillover is attenuated and $\eta$ comes out too high, which biases the answer toward the flattering side. The leakage rate should be reported, not assumed.
  • Generalisability. Effects estimated on restaurants that do not have professional photos today do not automatically apply to the installed base, which is a different population and a different decision.
